(1938) |Corylus iberica var. glandulosa|Kem.-Nath. (1938) |Corylus kachetica|Kem.-Nath. (1978) |Corylus macedonica|[[V.Cordus]] & [[Conrad Gessner|Gesner]] ex Strelin (1788) |Corylus nana|Tourrette & [[François Rozier|Rozier]] (1787) }} | synonyms_ref = }} '''''Corylus colurna''''', the '''Turkish hazel''', '''Byzantine hazel''' or '''Constantinople Hazel''', is a species of hazel (''[[Hazel|Corylus]]'') in the birch family ([[Betulaceae]]). It is native to the [[Balkans|Balkan Peninsula]] and [[West Asia|Western Asia]], but has become widely introduced in other areas of Europe as an [[Ornamental plant|ornamental]], particularly as a [[Urban forestry|street tree]]. It typically grows {{Convert|25-30|m|ft}} tall, with a slender growth form in its youth. Although the [[Hazelnut|nuts]] are not commercially important, ''Corylus colurna'' is commonly used as a single-stemmed, non-[[Basal shoot|suckering]] [[rootstock]] for common hazel (''[[Corylus avellana]]'') [[Grafting|scions]]. == Taxonomy == The genus ''Corylus'' is classified in the family Betulaceae, subfamily [[Coryloideae]], and is most closely related to ''[[Ostryopsis]], [[Hornbeam|Carpinus]]'', and ''[[Ostrya]]''. It is distributed in Europe, Western Asia, East Asia and North America, with 16 accepted species (as of August 2026).{{Cite web |title=Corylus L. {{!}} Plants of the World Online {{!}} Kew Science |url=http://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:13489-1 |access-date=2026-08-24 |website=Plants of the World Online |language=en}} ''Corylus colurna'' was among the 7,300 species |issn=1055-7903|url-access=subscription }} ==Description== It is a large species of [[hazel]], reaching {{convert|25|m|0|abbr=on}} tall,{{cite book | last=Rushforth | first=Keith | title=Trees of Britain and Europe | publisher=Trafalgar Square Publishing | publication-place=London | date=1999 | isbn=0-00-220013-9 | pages=190, 621–622}} exceptionally to {{cvt|33|m|0}} tall,{{cite web |last1=Todorov |first1=Atanas |title=Turkish Hazel west of Uzunalak, Kipilovo, Sliven, Bulgaria |url=https://www.monumentaltrees.com/en/bgr/sliven/kotel/38551_uzunalak/72461/ |website=Monumental Trees |access-date=28 December 2025}} with a stout trunk up to {{cvt|1|m|ft|0}} in diameter, rarely to {{cvt|1.6|m|ft|0}}. The crown is slender and conical in young trees, becoming broader and irregular with age. The [[Bark (botany)|bark]] is pale [[grey]]-[[buff (colour)|buff]], with a thick, [[cork (material)|corky]] texture. On young trees, the main limbs are quite small in diameter in relationship to the straight trunk, and arise at almost a 90-degree angle. This makes the tree suitable for urban conditions and helps maintain a symmetrical crown which is popular with landscape architects.{{cite web|first=Edward and Dennis|last=Gilman and Watson|title= ''Corylus colurna'' Fact Sheet| publisher=University of Florida |year=1993 |url=http://hort.ifas.ufl.edu/database/documents/pdf/tree_fact_sheets/corcola.pdf}} [[File:20140124Corylus colurna3.jpg|thumb|left|Twig in January with male (yellowish-brown) and female (red) catkins]] The [[leaf|leaves]] are [[deciduous]], rounded, {{Convert|7–13|cm|in|1}} long and {{cvt|6|–|14|cm|in|1}} across, softly hairy on both surfaces, and with a coarsely double-serrate to shallowly lobed margin. The buds are ovoid, pale brown. The [[flower]]s are produced in late winter or early spring before the leaves; the species is [[monoecy|monoecious]], with the individual [[catkin]]s single-sex, but both sexes on the same tree (and often on the same twig); the male catkins are conspicuous, pale yellow and 5–10 cm long, the female very small and inconspicuous, largely concealed in the buds, with only the bright red 1–3 mm long [[carpel|style]]s visible. The [[fruit]] is a [[Nut (fruit)|nut]] and may be known as the Turkish hazel nut, Turkish nut, or Constantinople nut. It is about 1–2 cm long, surrounded by a thick, softly spiny and bristly involucre (husk) 3 cm diameter, which encloses all but the tip of the nut; the nuts are borne in tight clusters of 3–8 together, with the involucres fused at the base. The fruit matures in September to October and is edible. Its taste is very similar to [[Corylus avellana|common hazel]], but it is smaller and has a thicker nut shell.{{cite web|title=''Corylus colurna''|publisher=University of Connecticut|url=http://www.hort.uconn.edu/plants/c/corcol/corcol1.html|access-date=2014-02-25|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140301222951/http://www.hort.uconn.edu/Plants/c/corcol/corcol1.html|archive-date=2014-03-01}} They are occasionally gathered from the wild as well as from urban trees, but their small size (smaller than common hazel nuts) and very hard, thick nut shell (3 mm thick) makes them of little or no commercial value. ''Corylus colurna'' is however important in commercial hazelnut [[orchard]]s, as it does not [[Basal shoot|sucker]], making it the ideal rootstock on which to [[grafting|graft]] the nut-bearing common hazel [[cultivar]]s. Nut production is irregular and occurs every two to three years Turkish Hazel. (n.d.) The Great Soviet Encyclopedia, 3rd Edition. (1970-1979). Retrieved 26 February 2014 from http://encyclopedia2.thefreedictionary.com/Turkish+Hazel === Root === ''Corylus colurna'' has fibrous roots.{{cite web|title=Guidelines for Tree Planting on the Right of Way|url=http://www.citywindsor.ca/residents/parksandforestry/Urban-Forest/Documents/Guidelines_for_Tree_Planting_o.pdf|publisher=City of Windsor}} The roots are not [[Adventitiousness|adventitious]], meaning they do not form suckers. This makes ''C. colurna'' desirable for grafting on the rootstock over a single stemmed trees. This allows it to be grown in poorer and rocky soils.Nikolva, M. (2007). Experimental results on variety-rootstock interaction in filbert culture. Notulae Botanicae Horti Agrobotanici Cluj-Napoca, 35(2), 82-87. ==Distribution and habitat== ''C. colurna'' is [[native plant|native]] to southeast Europe and southwest Asia, from the southern [[Balkans]] through northern [[Anatolia]] to the [[Caucasus]]. Although it has been reported from the mountain forests of northern [[Iran]] ([[Hyrcanian forests|Hyrcania]] and [[Turan]]) in the past, more recent surveys have failed to relocate it here, casting doubt over its continued presence in the region.{{Cite journal |last=Šeho |first=Muhidin |last2=Ayan |first2=Sezgin |last3=Huber |first3=Gerhard |last4=Kahveci |first4=Gülzade |date=2019-03-23 |title=A Review on Turkish Hazel (Corylus colurna L.) |url=https://www.seefor.eu/vol-10-no-1-seho-et-al-a-review-on-turkish-hazel-corylus-colurna.html |journal=South-east European forestry |language=en-gb |volume=10 |issue=1 |pages=53–63 |doi=10.15177/seefor.19-04 |issn=1849-0891|doi-access=free }} Previously, the species was also considered to be native to the [[western Himalayas]], but these populations are currently considered as constituting a different, though closely related species, ''[[Corylus jacquemontii|C. jacquemontii]].''{{Cite journal |last=Yang |first=Zhen |last2=Zhao |first2=Tian-Tian |last3=Ma |first3=Qing-Hua |last4=Liang |first4=Li-Song |last5=Wang |first5=Gui-Xi |date=2018-10-25 |title=Resolving the Speciation Patterns and Evolutionary History of the Intercontinental Disjunct Genus Corylus (Betulaceae) Using Genome-Wide SNPs |url=https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/plant-science/articles/10.3389/fpls.2018.01386/full |journal=Frontiers in Plant Science |language=English |volume=9 |doi=10.3389/fpls.2018.01386 |doi-access=free|issn=1664-462X |pmc=6209643 |pmid=30410496}} ''Corylus colurna'' occurs scattered in the mountains of the southern Balkans, the [[Pontic Mountains|Pontic Alps]] of northern Anatolia, the [[Armenian highlands|Armenian Highlands]], and the Caucasus. Although generally uncommon, it can be locally abundant in suitable sites. ''C. colurna'' occurs in a wide [[Altitudinal zonation|altitudinal range]] between 100 (in the Balkans) and 1,700 m (in the Caucasus) (330-5,680 ft), mostly on shallow, nutrient-poor lime soils. At lower altitudes, it constitutes a member [[Thermophile|thermophilous]] oak forests alongside, for example, Hungarian oak (''[[Quercus frainetto]]''), Oriental hornbeam (''[[Carpinus orientalis]]''), and flowering ash (''[[Fraxinus ornus]]''), whereas at higher elevations, it occurs together with beech (''[[Fagus sylvatica]]'', ''[[Fagus orientalis|F. orientalis]]'') and sycamore maple (''[[Acer pseudoplatanus]]''). It is light-demanding and relatively uncompetitive, becoming dominant only in very dry sites. In the Balkans, ''C. colurna'' is primarily distributed south of the Danube; the northernmost [[Native species|autochthonous]] stand grows in the [[southern Carpathians]] of Romania, close to the [[Iron Gates]]. It is also found in the [[Balkan Mountains|Balkan]], [[Sredna Gora]] and [[Rhodope Mountains]] of Bulgaria, the [[Pindus]] of Greece and Albania, and the [[Orjen]] in [[Bosnia and Herzegovina]], for example. In Anatolia, it occurs in a few scattered locations in the northwest and north (for example in [[Kastamonu Province|Kastamonu]]). In the Caucasus, it is primarily distributed in Georgia, but is also found in Armenia, for example near [[Getahovit]]. == Cultivation == ''Corylus colurna'' has a medium growth rate. It is occasionally drought tolerant and alkaline soil tolerant. However, it prefers moist, well-drained soil, as well as full sun. Once established ''C. colurna'' is tolerant of heat, cold, and drought. There are no serious pests or problems with ''C. colurna''.{{cite web| title=Turkish hazelnut| publisher=The Morton Arboretum| year=2013| url=http://www.mortonarb.org/trees-plants/tree-plant-descriptions/turkish-hazelnut}} ''Corylus colurna'' is not easily transplantable and will need extra watering in summer after transplanting. It will take about two years after transplant for the tree to become established and survive on its own.Phillips, L. (2002, July). Turkish Hazelnut. (Tree of the Month). Arbor Age, 22(7), 38. Retrieved from http://go.galegroup.com/ps/i.do?id=GALE%7CA89379137&v=2.1&u=sunycesfsc&it=r&p=PPAG&sw=w&asid=48a6ee3d38e80930f3a4add21f707a6d ''Corylus colurna'' has received the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]].{{cite web |url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/4517/Corylus-colurna/Details |title=''Corylus colurna'' |website=www.rhs.org |publisher=Royal Horticultural Society |access-date=12 April 2020}} ===Propagation=== The most common form of propagation is by seed. It is best sown as soon as it is harvested in autumn in a cold frame. The seed will germinate in late winter or spring. If starting with a stored seed, the seed should be pre-soaked in warm water for 48 hours and then given 2 weeks warm followed by 3 to 4 months cold stratification. This will allow the seed to germinate in 1 to 6 months if kept at 20 °C. Once the seedlings are large enough to handle, pick the seedlings out into individual pots and grow them on in a cold frame or sheltered place outdoors for their first winter. The seedlings can be planted into their permanent positions in late spring or early summer.L. (2013). Corylus colurna turkish hazel pfaf plant database. Retrieved from http://www.pfaf.org/user/plant.aspx?LatinName=Corylus colurna ==Uses== Besides its use as a single-stem rootstock for [[Corylus avellana|''C. avellana'']], ''C. colurna'' is widely cultivated as an ornamental tree in Europe and North America. It is very tolerant of difficult growing conditions in [[urban area|urban]] situations, which in recent decades has increased its popularity in civic planting schemes. Turkish hazel makes a good shade tree since it produces dense shade, and its narrow crown and ability to withstand air pollution make it well suited for use as a street tree in urban areas, or a specimen tree in parks. It makes a rather formal statement in the landscape due to the tight, consistently-shaped, narrow crown. Other landscape uses for ''C. colurna'' are for fruit, difficult and dry sites, and naturalistic areas. ==Gallery== File:Törökmogyoró.jpg|Foliage and immature fruit File:Baum Hasel, Corylus colurna 1.JPG|Involucre with ripe nut File:Involucre d'un noisetier de Bysance.jpg|Bristly involucre File:Corylus colurna0.jpg|A young Turkish hazel showing the narrow conical crown File:2015-05 ND-41 Baumhasel E-Leithe.jpg|Older specimens become broader, but often retain a good shape ==Related species== Similar species ''[[Corylus jacquemontii]]'', once considered as a variety of ''Coryllus colurna'', is found growing wild in the forests of Western Himalayan range in the north Indian state of [[Himachal Pradesh]] particularly in the temperate regions of districts of [[Kullu]], [[Shimla]], [[Kinnaur district]] and [[Chamba district]].Gupta and Sharma(2016).'''Site and stand characteristics of hazelnut bearing forests in temperate region of Himachal Pradesh'''.International Journal of Farm Sciences'.
